newsitem.title: USA: Florida judge set precedent in stadium ruling.
newsitem.headline: Florida judge set precedent in stadium ruling.

text.p: A Florida judge set a precedent and sent a warning to other professional sports teams when he ruled that the Tampa Bay Buccaneers' new stadium agreement was primarily for private gain, a sports economist said Monday.
"I think we can expect to see this particular case cited in the future," said Robert Baade, a professor of economics at Lake Forest College in Illinois.
"I think leagues have been put on notice that they just can't demand the moon, the sun, the sky and the stars from cities. They have to temper some of these demands," Baade said.
Circuit Judge Sam Pendino refused Friday to validate a $204.5 million tax-exempt revenue bond issue for the stadium by the Tampa Sports Authority.

The judge said a lease provision giving the team the first $2 million of annual revenues from non-Bucs events at the stadium made the project one primarily for private gain, and that it would be unconstitutional to issue tax-backed bonds for that purpose.

Nelson Luis, a spokesman for the Bucs, said team officials were still reviewing the ruling Monday and had met with City of Tampa and Hillsborough County officials. But he said there had been no decision on whether the team would try to renogitiate the lease with the city, county and sports authority.
"They were trying to figure out exactly what the ruling meant, what course of action they will take," Luis said.
Baade is the author of a previous study that concluded publicly financed stadiums and arenas mainly benefit team owners and players, not the public.
He testified during the Florida hearing for the plaintiff, former Tampa Mayor Bill Poe, who sought to block the bond issue on constitutional grounds.
"This is the first time really that we had a stadium under construction that was stopped," Baade said.
He said Pendino's ruling sent a message that, "When you do these public use things, this has to somehow serve a public purpose."

Construction began on the stadium last fall, after Hillsborough County voters approved a one-cent sales tax increase to finance schools, public safety projects and the stadium. City officials said that unless the bonds are issued, the stadium authority would run out of money for the project by mid to late April.
